subtopic: STEEL EXPORTS-EFFECT OF UNITED STATES LEGISLATION
STEEL EXPORTS-EFFECT OF UNITED STATES LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the people of Hamilton and all those concerned with the Canadian steel industry, to express my regret over the Government's inaction with respect to the United States Trade and Tariff Act (1984). If this law goes into effect, steel products entering the United States will be required to have their country of origin stamped on them. This new, non-tariff barrier will cost the Canadian industry millions of dollars to comply with, and risk those markets where unmarked steel is required. This will end up costing Canadians steel jobs.
There was a presentation made last week at the Canadian Embassy to U.S. Customs officials about the implications of these new regulations. The Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) was visibly absent from this presentation. If the Government is at all concerned about this issue, then the very least it could do is to have the Minister personally lead the lobby to protect Canadian jobs. I might add that in the document presented this week discussing international trade, the whole steel question was left completely untouched, another indication of the Government's disinterest and lack of commitment on this issue.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) claims the Government is approaching the issue with vigour, but its actions fall far short. I believe the Canadian Government should start to take a tougher stand with the U.S. Government on this issue and stop the smoke and mirrors approach which has been taken to date, before thousands of steel jobs in Hamilton, Sault Ste. Marie, Nova Scotia, and across the country are lost.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT DECISION-POSITION OF SMALL RETAILERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to congratulate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on his decision regarding metric conversion.
As a defender of consumer interests and as someone who, as former President of the Association des services de l'automo-bile du Quebec, has been involved for many years in these issues, I think this is a real victory for the small retailer. It is the first time any Minister has shown so much consideration for the interests of small retail businesses. I therefore wish to thank the Minister on behalf of all small retailers in Quebec and across Canada.
The Minister, in his wisdom, has been careful to consider the interests and wishes of the majority of intervenors in this controversial issue. This will be an opportunity for small retailers to better identify with consumer needs without having to ask the permission of the multinationals first. From now on, they will be free of this obligation.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO LIFE'S WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday our country lost a truly magnificent human being. Frank Scott, poet, professor of constitutional law, champion of civil rights, and a social democrat, died at his home in Westmount.
This "rebel without a pause" took on and defeated Maurice Duplessis in a historic civil rights battle that we now know as the Padlock case.
In the words of Tommy Douglas, he was the Canadian intellectual stimulus of the 1930s and 1940s.
His friend and associate, Charles Taylor, describes Frank Scott in these words: "He was this very strange and wonderful mixture of very high social and political aspiration with this streak of clear eyed perception of human failings, all with a sense of humour."
He was the two-time winner of the Governor General's award for literature, and by his actions and deeds he influenced the course of history. As fellow poet Louis Dudek said: "I feel he is going to rise to mythical greatness."
February 1, 1985

In Frank Scott's own words:
From those condemned to labour For profit of another We take our new endeavour.
For sect and class and pattern Through whom the strata harden We sharpen now the weapon.
Till power is brought to pooling And outcasts share in ruling There will not be an ending Nor any peace for spending.
On behalf of my colleagues, and I hope on behalf of the House of Commons and the people of Canada, we express to his wife Marian, and his son Peter, our condolences, and a grateful thanks for the inspiration that he was.

subsubtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF YALTA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Monday, February 4 will begin the fortieth anniversary of the Yalta Conference. In 1945, at that Crimean centre, President Roosevelt, Prime Minister Churchill, and Marshal Stalin met for eight days to plan what would follow victory. Yalta was one of the most significant summit meetings in the 20th century. It led to the bifurcation of Europe by that iron curtain which still shuts eastern Europe off from the West.
I speak of it in the House of Commons because of all the Canadians who trace their heritage back to those countries still dominated by the Red Army. Many of these Canadians are to be found in Scarborough, as they are in most of our communities. In the past 17 years many people have wondered where the Canadian Government stood on the Soviet threat to their homelands. In 1985, the fortieth anniversary of Yalta, let there be no doubt that Canada still looks for that time when the Red Star will not fill the sky over eastern Europe.

subsubtopic: CORPORATE TAX BREAKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the main themes of last summer's election was the issue of fair taxation. Specifically at issue was the level of tax loopholes and opportunities for tax deferrals which were allowed for large corporations in the mistaken belief that they would
February 1, 1985

trickle down to provide jobs for ordinary Canadians. In response to this agenda, which was set by the New Democratic Party, the then Minister of Finance was quoted as saying that a thorough review of tax breaks for private industry was needed "to determine where the system is being abused". subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF NAMES OF PERSONS CHARGED WITH SEXUAL OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an issue of importance to the people of my riding of Niagara Falls, and to the people of this country, that is, the practice of publishing the names of individuals who are charged with Criminal Code offences. We are all aware of the devastating effects this can have, not only on the individual, but on the friends and relatives of the accused as well. In the public's eye the presumption of innocence may be lost. It is little comfort that the accused may establish his innocence at some point in the future. The damage has been done.
Recently in the city of St. Catharines, 32 individuals were charged with the commission of sexual offences. Their names were immediately made public. The loss of reputation and the anguish are a high price to pay. I would suggest it is too high a price without a conviction.
It is pointed out that there may be a restriction of the public's right to know, or of the freedom of the press. Those are important rights that should never be treated lightly. However, there is the right of the individual, and his protection should be paramount. Therefore, I would urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), my colleagues on the Justice Committee, and other Members of the House to consider amendments to the Criminal Code that would prohibit the publication of an accused's name unless there is a conviction.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF BAHA'I BELIEVERS IN IRAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my concern with respect to the future of the Baha i faith in Iran. The 300,000 members of the Baha'i faith have been denied recognition under the Iranian constitution, and are now being persecuted as an entire community.
Unless their problem receives recognition, the Baha'is could eventually cease to exist as a distinct entity and face the same fate which the Falasha Jews almost encountered in Ethiopia.
The Toronto Star reported on January 30 that Iran has become the first country to denounce the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, effectively shutting off current United Nations investigations into any claims.
The Baha'is are expressly forbidden by their religion to take part in politics, and are commanded to obey civilian authorities, thus posing no threat to Iran.
On behalf of the Baha'i community in Toronto, Canada, and the rest of the world, I urge the Government of Canada to take initiatives in the international community to ensure that the Baha'is are not discriminated against in Iran.

February 1, 1985

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to introduce my first Bill in the House today.
Under this Bill, people enrolling in a course or training program of their choice, at their own expense, will be eligible to receive benefits as provided under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, subject to approval by the Commission. Unlike those people who take a course at the Commission's expense, this group, under the present legislation, is denied the privilege of receiving unemployment insurance benefits because they are considered not available for employment.
Furthermore, the Bill provides that a person whose appeal to the board of referees is maintained may receive unemployment insurance benefits from the date of his initial application to the Commission. This means we will be able to eliminate the discrimination created by the previous Government against people who want to improve their situation.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, January 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Masse that Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak in the House today on this Bill which deals with the Broadcasting Act and the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission.
Thanks to the electors in my riding, I represent the constituency of Calgary West in the House. That riding disappeared for many years through the process of redistribution and came back into being in 1979. I have had the pleasure of representing it since that time. A previous incumbent of that riding was the Hon. Prime Minister R. B. Bennett. It was a Conservative Government and that particular Prime Minister who in 1932 brought forward the concept that the Canadian air waves should be regulated. That was an important feature of the Canadian identity. Through the regulation of those air waves we had an opportunity to develop something distinctly Canadian. It is certainly important to those of us who are fortunate enough to live in this country.
I want to pay tribute to that event of 52 years ago. In 1984 the riding of Calgary West is as concerned about the development of a Canadian identity and culture as it was in 1932 when R. B. Bennett had the honour of representing the people of that region.
As I sat here yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I become more and more distraught about the consistency with which Members of both opposition Parties used the debate on this Bill to discuss the issue of budgetary cuts and specifically those applying to the CBC. Anyone who has taken the trouble to read the Bill
CRTC Act
knows that it has nothing to do with those cuts. Yet the House was abused by those who chose to drag that red herring into this debate.
The piece of legislation before us is important and should be moved forward with dispatch. Unfortunately, Members of the Opposition left this Chamber, and perhaps some people in the country, with a false impression about the cuts.
I would like to take a minute or two to remind Members of the Opposition and Canadians that the Government was changed on September 4, 1984 partly because the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party refused to deal with the financial reality of this country. They refused to recognize that if you take in $400 every couple of weeks and spend $600, you are running a deficit. The Canadian deficit is in that ratio. We are taking in two-thirds of what we spend. We are spending one-third more than we take in. If a family took in $400 a week and spent $600 a week, in four weeks' time it would be $800 in debt. Every four weeks it would be $800 more in debt and would have to pay the interest on that debt.
When I was elected in 1979, Mr. Speaker, 83 cents of every tax dollar collected could be spent for good purpose and 17 cents was spent on interest. After five and one-half years of bad economic management only 65 cents of every tax dollar collected can be spent for useful purposes. The difference is the interest payments.
Who suffers because of that massive deficit which no one seems to have the political will to control? The unemployed who have no income are prejudiced by the deficit. The senior citizens and others on fixed incomes are prejudiced by the deficit. When a government borrows to the extent that the Liberals were borrowing, interest rates go up, the cost of living goes up, inflation runs away and people on fixed income are hurt. Furthermore, our children are the ones who will have to pay for that borrowing. Our children are having their future income cut because this debt is passed on to them.
I hope the opposition Parties have heard the message that the Canadian voters have given to them. Canadians understand that there is no free lunch and that all of the activities of the Government must be reviewed in order to determine what services are essential and where cuts could be applied. I will stand in the Chamber as often as necessary to urge the Government to make those cuts where necessary, but to do so with sensitivity and compassion in order to bring the fiscal affairs of this country back to a reasonable state. We can no longer spend more than we receive.
The CBC is a specific example of such overspending. It is wrong to believe that that corporation is not wasteful in its operations. While I do not believe anyone knows how much waste there is, a reasonable government would require the corporation to find that waste and eliminate it. That is what this Government is doing.
I also suggest that the CBC cuts have been in the Government subsidy. The Government cuts the subsidy, not the CBC's budget. I suggest that the CBC has additional income

February 1, 1985
CRTC Act
opportunities which it can find if it is aggressive. It can maintain its budget by increasing its current income. If the corporation can produce its own quality English or French programming it can penetrate other markets around the world and thereby generate its own revenue. Moreover, the programming will meet our cultural goals. Furthermore, the CBC should be aggressively looking for increased sponsorship. It cannot always depend on the will of the taxpayers of this country to meet all of its requests.
In effect, I am saying that I believe the cuts to the CBC are necessary and have been managed sensitively. I believe the corporation has alternative ways to meet its mandate and I want the record to be clear that I support the direction taken by the Government in regard to the cuts.
Let me move now to the legislation.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: I was going to ask about that.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: In French!

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
French or English, it is the same thing. [English]
This piece of legislation is a classical example that shows the difference between how the opposition parties operated and the way the Conservative Government said it would operate. Bill C-20 deals with the CRTC and broadcasting generally. It does not mention the Film Development Corporation, the CBC or Bell Canada. While new Members may not notice that difference, it is apparent to me because the former Liberal Government continually introduced legislation in the form of omnibus Bills. It brought forward a package of measures similar to what we are dealing with today which not only dealt with broadcasting but with the CBC, Bell Telephone and the Canadian Film Development Corporation. The Liberal Government would then ask Members of the House to cast a single vote on the principle of such a Bill.
I suggest that those are four separate topics for which there indeed may be four separate principles. It is not possible to cast a single vote for such omnibus legislation, and one of the reasons the Liberals are in opposition today is that they continually attempted to deny Parliament the basic principles of democracy. They introduced omnibus legislation that did not address a specific principle. The bells rang for 17 days and they were defeated in an election on the basic principle of whether or not democracy was being served.
When the debate on second reading of this Bill is finished, we will be able to vote on the principle of its benefit to broadcasting generally while not dealing with Bell Telephone, CBC or the Film Development Corporation. I congratulate the Government for fulfilling that commitment.
How does this legislation differ from the previous Act? I believe its most fundamental principle would provide Parliament with the ultimate authority to direct the policy of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. Without such a principle the CRTC consists of a group of
appointed people who can set national policy. Once they are appointed they are accountable to no one and cannot be recalled. I believe it was a mistake to establish such a principle originally and I want to commend the Government for so carefully enshrining in these changes the basic principle that those who are accountable to the voters of the country will be responsible for determining the policy. We, as the elected representatives of the people, will be able to advise that appointed body about how to proceed.
I believe this basic principle is even more important today, given the explosion of technology. It may be necessary in the next four years of this Parliament to use that principle as we move through the VCR revolution, the satellite dish revolution and so on. There may be continued need to update and amend the policy so that Canadian culture is enhanced and the Canadian identity is strengthened through proper utilization of new technology as it comes on stream. That is the first principle and the most important one.
There is a second principle which I commend to the Opposition. The Opposition may have a knee-jerk reaction to it, but I ask opposition Members to pause. The second important principle of this Bill is that it changes the legislation in a manner that will ensure the Commission does not have to regulate new situations where a competitive market exists. The CRTC can get out of the business of regulating.
Think for a moment, Mr. Speaker, about the costs that are always inherent in the regulatory process. For instance, appearing before hearings and the costs that are always inherent in meeting the conditions that come about through regulation. If there is a saving of 1 per cent, 2 per cent, 10 per cent or whatever that currently goes into paperwork, that can be eliminated, and the money saved used for programming, then this nation will be the better for it. I am really pleased to see that principle in this legislation. I anticipate seeing a similar principle in many pieces of legislation that will be brought before this Parliament.
We have been too long governed by a political philosophy and a political party that believed it knew best, that put in place increased numbers of regulatory bodies and increased numbers of regulations that have become a drain on the national economy and national will. They are too expensive in economic terms and too expensive in psychological terms because of the impact they have on the spirit of people. I am pleased to be able to stand in this place today and support that portion of the Bill that allows us not to regulate. It is a sad commentary that we have to have wording like that. It really speaks to the underlying philosophical persuasion which has governed our affairs in previous times, and it will be changed.
I am also pleased to see that those who become licensees will be granted a seven-year period rather than a five-year period. If I am critical at all, maybe it should be 10 years. Maybe it should be forever with a mechanism that allows it to be revoked when it is abused. Certainly seven years is better than five years. People can plan with confidence, they can be more
February 1, 1985

efficient and more effective. They will only have to use money to make application every seven years instead of five years. Even that saving can be put into programming. I hope the Government with the passage of time will consider going further.
There is another principle which is in accord with the Charter of Rights and the will of the people of this House. I think as a group we might have unanimity here. None of us wants to see the air waves used for abusive purposes, for purposes which degrade women, children, men, different racial groups, different religions and different ethnic groups. The air waves should not be used for abusive purposes and I am pleased to see that the Government is providing a mechanism to control the situation. I encourage the committee to study the wording of the Bill carefully. We want no denial of the freedom of speech; we simply want to be sure that the wording provides the mechanism necessary to stop that abuse.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I think the French CBC network can have an impact on the French culture because of its high quality programs. In my opinion, the French CBC network is now better than anything TV viewers can watch in France.

It can work both ways. Canadian programmers, authors, actors and writers are of sufficient quality that it is time we began to look outwards and to be less afraid of others influencing us. It is time to begin to look at the opportunities for us to influence them. If we make that shift in our mind-set, say that we are a strong nation with talented people and realize that we have something to offer the world, then we can begin to look at whether or not a piece of legislation advances or retards that aim.
In terms of regulation, this piece of legislation does not remove the power to regulate. It removes the necessity to regulate so that each situation can be looked at as to whether or not regulation might enhance or retard the situation. It is that principle which I support not only here but everywhere. If there is one certitude which flows from regulation, it is the certitude that it uses up resources and costs money to go through the process and meet the conditions. If it is unnecessary in the first place, surely it frees up money for the creative process. I think we will find agreement in the Chamber that in this field we should do whatever we can to enhance and produce money for the creative process. If that is the case, we are moving in the right direction. If we can take money away from the administrative or paperwork side of it and put it into the creative side, we will have done something for the country. I believe this Bill moves in that direction. That is one of the reasons we should support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also want to thank my colleagues for their courtesy in letting me take the floor again in the House. I am pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words and express a few ideas on Bill C-20 concerning the-

In examining any legislation which is put before the Chamber, we should not only look at what is laid down or projected in the legislation. We should also consider what is not specified in it and, therefore, what is assumed-that which might be changed but is not being changed.
The most significant characteristic of this legislation is that it envisages the continuation of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. That is a decision about which I personally have a few minor reservations but not one with which I fundamentally disagree.
The CRTC is an example of what my friends in England would call a quango, a quasi-autonomous non-governmental organization.

I do not know whether there is a French translation for this word. It is quite popular over there.

Essentially quangos are established to accomplish for the Government what it deems to be too controversial, burdensome or inexpedient for it to tackle individually as a matter of the policy process. In the opinion of those who have observed and analysed them, they are a mechanism which is very much open to misuse and excessive use in terms of allowing them to undertake responsibilities which might properly be left with the Government.
Nevertheless, the CRTC, particularly over the earlier years of its life, did not attract a great deal of controversy. However,
February 1, 1985

I bring to the attention of Hon. Members of the House the degree of dissatisfaction which has existed about the CRTC in many rural and remote areas of Canada. Perhaps I will expand on that later in my discourse.
Like many similar organizations, the CRTC has been the target of or, shall we say, opportunity for the patronage process. We have seen appointments to that Commission which would be difficult to justify on any objective evaluation of the qualifications of the people so appointed. Nevertheless we acknowledge that there are many who have made a good start and have made good progress with that Commission. There is no pretence that under the present structure of the CRTC it can set policy for the Government. Because of the pace of technology and the way in which developments have proceeded, there have indeed been occasions on which policy laid down by the CRTC did effectively make policy for the Government. Decisions of the CRTC made policy for the Government whether they liked it or not.
I am reminded somewhat of the Hound of the Baskervilles and the classic exchange between Holmes and Watson when discussing what happened about the dog. Holmes said: "Remember, Watson, the curious incident of the dog in the night-time." To which Watson replied: "The dog did nothing in the night-time." "Ah," said Holmes, "that was the curious incident". There have been occasions when the CRTC did function much as the dog in the night-time and did not do what it might legitimately have been expected to undertake.
We in this Party support the introduction of the clause which gives the Government the right to direct the CRTC to take a certain question, issue or problem under its mandate. By judicious and responsible use of that clause, the Government can indeed prevent the CRTC from being further perceived as the dog in the night-time.
If this power is passed into law, we would certainly enjoin the Government to use it carefully, responsibly and, above all, sparingly. Like any other body in its meetings, the Commission members form an impression of what they should be doing. The introduction of items that were not previously on their agenda is something that can be disruptive to the ongoing functions. In taking the power unto itself, we hope the Government will use it with some responsibility and, as I have said, on a relatively infrequent basis.
I should like to turn to Section 14.6 which gives the Minister the power to exclude a service or activity from regulatory control on the basis that competition is sufficient to ensure just and reasonable rates. I take issue with the previous speaker, whether he be now present or absent, and say that that is a power that we in this Party feel is open to some question and potentially open to some abuse. It is not a power that we like to see in this Bill.
We believe that the regulatory process can be streamlined, such that a mandate of oversight, review, observation and supervision need not take a great deal of resources and need not overly tax the Commission. The power to exempt a par-
CRTC Act
ticular activity, market or service from the Commission's supervision is one that might be open to abuse. It might in fact be used in such a way that it could create loopholes.
It is assured that there are many industries in which the competitive environment changes overnight. We remember the bank amalgamations of the 1920s and the 1930s which reduced effectively the number of chartered banks in Canada from something in the hundreds to a total of five. Because there is no mention of reinstatement or reversal of such an exemption, we would question the usefulness and the appropriateness of that clause.
I now turn to the matter of the proposed amendment to Section 3 of the Broadcasting Act requiring all programming to promote the equality and dignity of all persons. I personally and my Party are strongly in favour of such an amendment, but if it be inserted in there, it must have teeth. Under the present programming regime, and indeed present state protocol, we would find instant violations. We have a national anthem which states "true patriot love in all thy sons command". This should properly be changed if it were to conform with the proposed amendment to Section 3. Promoting the equality and dignity of all persons is a laudable objective; however, it must be supported by concrete stipulations in the amended Act. It is an objective that is too often the subject of too much lip service within this country and not enough action.
My own concern is specifically with the pornography of violence which I see as being an abuse and, in effect, an assault not only on women, although I affirm that they are the most frequently chosen victims, but also on children and indeed on men. I have no argument with the sincere depiction of the act of love. I have no argument with the depiction of naked forms, be they male or female. But I am concerned that under present programming regimes, particularly as regards some of the imported material from our neighbour to the south, we are allowing a depiction of violence, a depiction of hostility between persons that is in danger of creating in the generation that grows up with television, as I and many others did not do, the belief that violence, verbal and physical assault, hostility- sometimes even worse than we find in this Chamber-is the common currency of every day dealings between people.
The matter of satellite dishes is something that came very close to my heart during the election campaign and, of course, since. There was a situation in the community of Red Lake where over a thousand residents were joint members in an enterprise that set up a satellite dish. It was seized on the orders of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. I am pleased by the task force that was established on the distribution in underserved communities of satellite-received broadcasting services. That task force is scheduled to report on February 11.
I look forward to a report that will satisfy the legitimate aspirations of Canadians in remote communities, the legitimate needs and expression of the desire for not only cultural programming, but also the full range of programming that is available to many southern, and urban communities.

I support the representations of the Satellite TV Associations of Canada, although in many ways I have to take issue with some of the tactics that were used. When the law does allow for the seizure of equipment without compensation, it is not surprising that people get upset.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with this opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-20 a very important piece of legislation to amend the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act.
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware, this Bill or at least a very similar one was introduced in the House by the Liberal Party during the last Parliament. I think it would be useful to provide a quick review of the Bill's history, and I am sure Hon. Members would be very upset if I did not take advantage of this opportunity.
On February 8, 1984, the previous Liberal Minister introduced legislation on telecommunications and broadcasting. Subsequently, a number of representations were made by various parties including women's groups and on May 24, 1984, amendments were made to the Bill. These amendments dealt with the principle of equality and personal dignity and were included in the Bill. On May 29, 1984, the same Minister announced a national film and video policy dealing with cultural as well as economic interests. And here ends my brief review.
Now, however, we see the Government introducing a similar Bill in the House. I was a little surprised, Mr. Speaker, that when the Minister introduced this Bill, he did not have the courtesy to mention the excellent work done by his predecessor. Only this morning, we heard the Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) saying how important this Bill was and
that it was an excellent initiative and so on. I therefore wish to thank the Member for Calgary West for recognizing this Liberal initiative by the previous Government, and I am sure that when Mr. Fox reads his speech in Hansard, he will be very pleased with what the Hon. Member for Calgary West had to say about him. I think it is important to understand this.
Mr. Speaker, this morning, the Member for Calgary West spent quite some time informing the House that Hon. Members should not take advantage of the debate on this Bill to discuss budgetary cutbacks in telecommunications. He then went on to spend ten minutes explaining that the cutbacks were reasonable, after informing the House that the subject was not a suitable one. Mr. Speaker, since a precedent was created this morning, I am sure you will agree that I should be allowed to say a few words about this subject, in response to what was said by the Hon. I would like to speak about the Bill itself. I come from a riding that will be affected by this legislation. There are sections of the legislation which I must applaud. I do not agree with everything in the legislation, but there are some ideas which have been a long time coming. I agree that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) should have the power to give policy direction to the CRTC. This is often necessary within the CRTC or the CTC. I see that the Minister of

Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) is in the Elouse. There is often a Government commission which makes unpopular decisions. We ask questions in the House of the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Communications and are told that that was not done by them but by the CRTC, the CTC or some other body which happens to be filled with Government supporters. It is essential that the elected Ministers make the policy decisions and take responsibility for them. We support that particular change in the legislation.
However, as a caveat to my earlier remarks, I wish to say that it is important that there still be a forum through which those people affected by such measures have an opportunity to make their representations known. The CRTC has performed such a role over the years whereby people who were affected by certain applications would be able to appear at a hearing before the CRTC to make representations.
1 hope that when the Government makes decisions about cutting back services or encouraging private enterprise to the exclusion of the CBC it will also provide a forum for those citizens affected by those decisions to make presentations. I must say that I do not believe that that is necessarily a job for the committees of the House of Commons because most of them do not travel. Commissions such as the CRTC and the Canadian Transport Commission are able to travel to the areas affected by applications. We hope that the CRTC will continue to play a role in hearing evidence from concerned groups affected by policy on the future of communications in this country.
There is another aspect of this legislation that concerns me. In areas where the Minister believes there is enough competition in the future, the CRTC would lose its power to make regulatory decisions. I am not convinced that there is much competition with regard to communications. Most communities across this country have only one or two stations serving them. Most people who subscribe to a cable network only receive one cable network. Therefore, we should realize that there is not a lot of competition in the communications business in this country and it is necessary to have a regulatory body which will retain the authority to hear submissions not only about price but the level of service being provided to the various communities. If this clause is put into law, I hope there will not be many exclusions from the regulatory process which has generally served us well in the past.
My riding covers the northern two-thirds of Manitoba. It covers 186,000 square miles and consists of 50 communities. One study which will affect my riding is that by the CRTC special task force on service to small, isolated communities. One of our difficulties in speaking to this legislation presently is that we do not have the findings of that task force at the present time. When we are speaking on a Bill which affects the future communications policy of the Government and the direction which communications will be taking, it is unfortunate that we do not have that information before us at the present time.
This has been a problem in the past because this aspect of communications is one for which rules that were set up for the CRTC were really meant for larger communities with greater numbers competing for licences and areas where inexpensive cable systems can be established. These are areas where Canadians live close to the American border and are already able to receive extra service.
The problem faced by northern and smaller communities was that they either received no television or radio or perhaps only received one network, which was the CBC in most cases. The CBC had a mandate to serve smaller towns while the private enterprise networks, by their own admission, did not see a profit in providing a television or radio service to communities such as those in my riding and those in the riding of my colleague, the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
The advent of the satellite dish provided the capability to pick signals out of the air. As a result, many of these communities became involved in what was called illegal broadcasting. For example, one of the first satellite dishes in Canada, certainly in northern Manitoba, was brought in by a reserve in my riding, Red Sucker Lake. That reserve did not even have CBC service, let alone any other service. The chief and council took $60,000 from funds that were raised from various sources such as bingo and sports and bought a satellite dish. It picked up signals for free and provided broadcasting to the residents of that reserve. Although it was illegal, it was the only way they could get any television service.
That system mushroomed throughout the North and the rest of the country. In reaction to the situation the Cancom satellite network was set up whereby legal service was provided which could be used by many of those northern communities. However, that is a very expensive service to provide. One of the inequities that exists at this time is that larger cities such as Winnipeg have fairly reasonable rates, such as $6.40 a month for cable service, while the poor, small communities in my riding must pay $19.20 a month or more to get the Cancom satellite service. Many of the people in those communities are unemployed and do not have a lot of money.
When the task force makes its recommendations it should find ways of providing good Canadian service, because we need a service which guarantees a minimum of Canadian content. Certainly there is enough Canadian content available, with Ontario educational TV, the CBC and some of the programs coming from the National Film Board. However, it should also consider the price of that service. I hope that report takes the provision of cheaper service into consideration for the eventual regulations.
We should also recognize that the people who live in smaller communities do not have the same entertainment options as those who live in Winnipeg, Regina, Toronto or Montreal. Quite often they are tempted to pick up illegal satellite reception of channels which cover sports or movies, such as the Home Box Office, because they do not have professional hockey in their communities, and many communities in my riding do not have movie theatres. The only way they can see

I believe the CBC has done a good job in the past and Canadian content is important to keep the cultural identity of this nation. However, we must also recognize that these people live in communities where the entertainment options are very limited. They have a greater need for a variety of programming than people in some of the larger areas and cities of this country.

There is an increasing level of violence in television programs coming into this country. For the most part they are not Canadian-based programs. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the Hon. Member survived his luncheon with the various people who are concerned about the CBC and I hope the CBC survives this Government.
With regard to the substantive matter which the Parliamentary Secretary has brought up, whether the CRTC, the Canadian Transport Commission or others should have an independent policy-making role, I believe that will always be the case to some degree anyway. They will be in a situation of finding it very difficult to get service in the future. Some will say that is an administrative matter. I would say that when the Government cuts services affecting one language or cultural group in the country, in effect it is setting a policy or it is following an existing government policy. It is a bit more than administration.
I can speak with some experience as I used to be the vice-chairman of the Manitoba Police Commission. Even though the Government of Manitoba set a policy, the decisions of the Police Commission or any other commission in the decision-making process somehow established policy for the future. It is a balancing act. I hope the Government sets the general policy so that we in the House can rise and question the Minister as to policy directions and express our concerns to various Ministers, whether it be the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) or whoever. At the same time there are other citizens and interest groups out there who need something like the

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on the address of the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). I particularly appreciate his remarks in the latter part of his speech when he referred to the need of the community at large to hear and to feel the impact of the CRTC in a very local sense. Clearly, that is what has been missing in the past.
I should like to refer to some small communities in the Slocan Valley such as New Denver and Silverton, communities of that nature. They are a very isolated area where the geography is vertical instead of horizontal. When their permits expired for the rebroadcast of a Canadian channel-and at that time it was the CBC-they were told by the CRTC that they would not be relicensed. When CRTC officials came to me to describe the reason for that decision, they suggested that perhaps the little town of New Denver should put in a television studio to broadcast from the community at the base of the mountain where no signals were available, so that the people in that community could receive television. Those are the kinds of things which have been alluded to that make absolutely no sense. They demonstrate that the Government and the bureaucracy at the time were totally out of touch with the people. There is a telephone line going right by its door. It carries the signal of CBC Radio. They cannot listen to it. These 300 people have radios which do not have sufficient strength to pick up CBC Radio, yet the CBC signal runs on the telephone line by its door. They cannot tap into it. I suppose they could do so if they were millionaires. However, the bottom line is that the rate which the B.C. Telephone Company wants for the service is so astronomical that there is no point in even considering it for a community of some 300 people.

of Communications, the Hon. Francis Fox, nor are my reservations about Bill C-20 to be found in its wording, although there are some important omissions in it and amendments are needed.
My reservations are more fundamental than that. When amendments were written under the Liberal administration, we assumed that there was an absolute understanding by all- and this was right and reasonable-that the Government would continue the arm's length policy of not interfering with the CRTC, the CBC or, for that matter, with cultural and arts councils. That was always Liberal Government policy, and it was written at the time. The Liberal Government at that time assumed that that relationship would continue. However, I now have strong reservations after only six months of rule by the Tory Government. All indications are that the Government and the Conservative Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) have a different approach and a different agenda in mind.
On November 29, 1984 The Globe and Mail indicated that the Tory Minister of Communications said that he wanted to rethink the arm's length policy and that his Government was moving rapidly to apply a direct political hand into the affairs of the agency, the CBC. He hired three private consultants to advise him on the fate of the CBC. He interposed political agents into the CBC situation and asked them to monitor and, I imagine, to manipulate. This has already been brought to the attention of the House by my Liberal colleagues.
Another proof of flagrant government interference is by hands on manipulation-by putting its hands on the throat of the CBC to strangle it Financially, to force it and to intimidate it, to make it tremble and conform to Tory Government objectives. Imagine the ramifications of Bill C-20, if it is put into force now, in the hands of this Minister and this Government.
How can we trust the Government with power of direction of the CRTC? How can we trust it in light of the facts? In the few short months the Government has been in power, it has created more havoc and chaos among the cultural and artistic community than any foreign invader could have done in as many years. By its massive and ill-considered budgetary cuts to the CBC and to numerous arts and cultural organizations in the country, the Government has created distrust, fear and consternation among broadcasters, writers, artists, musicians and communicators of all kind who give us a sense of our own identity. Our feeling of national identity is now being threatened. The cuts the Government has made to the CBC will result in a serious blow to Canadian programming. CBC management has virtually conceded this.
I ask the Government how it can go on reducing Canadian programming at a time when the cultural sovereignty of our air waves is being threatened as never before. I remind the Government that it was its own Party which originally founded the CBC with the following words:
This country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources... free from foreign interference or influence.

Why, then, is the Government actively behaving as if it wants our air waves to be filled with American programming? Does it know that two major documentaries have recently been aired in Europe devoted exclusively to discussing the pathetic and tragic situation that is occurring in the Canadian television situation?
Does this Government realize that on any evening of the week, only 23 per cent of the programs over television have any Canadian content whatever? Does it know that for every hour of Canadian drama seen in this country, 24 hours of American drama is broadcast? Finally, if it is aware of all this, why is it carrying out a policy that will make a bad situation even worse?
The record of this new Conservative Government in broadcasting is one that no true Canadian, no Canadian with any sense of feeling for this country and what it stands for, can support. By slashing the operating budgets of the CBC, the National Film Board, the Canada Council and all other institutions which we rely on to give us our sense of identity, the Government has thrown away any credibility it may have had as a defender of our national dreams.
It is this Party's forerunner that created the national dream by building a railroad across this country. We now see the sorry side of this very same Party destroying a national dream of another kind, a national dream of a Canadian identity expressed through the artists and their broadcasters.
This Government cannot be trusted to control broadcasting. It has shown that in a few short months. It slashed the central pillar of our broadcasting system, the CBC, so deeply and indiscriminately that it is in mortal danger. Given the record of this Government and its shameful betrayal of our national dream, our expression of our Canadian identity, given the record of betrayal of public broadcasting by this Government, we must not allow it to gain even more control over broadcasting by means of this Bill.

There have been massive cuts to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which have been widely decried as hasty and ill-considered. The $85 million cut to the CBC has needlessly created 1,200 unemployed broadcasters at the CBC. In addition, hundreds of independent contributors to the Corporation are now without a source of income.

The CBC appropriation spends over $15 million every year on musicians and composers in this country. No one else

Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to defend the relevance of what I am saying on Bill C-20. It will be seen, if one reviews the text of what I have said, that I have been establishing a very simple principle. I said at the outset that Bill C-20 as written would have no problems within it if the Government operated on the basis of an arm's length relationship. That was the assumption when this Bill was first introduced. It was based on the assumption of an arm's length relationship.
I am establishing that in every area the Minister and the Government are not carrying out an arm's length relationship with the arts, the CBC and other cultural organizations for which the CRTC presumably is responsible. If this Bill passes and it defines for the CRTC its areas of responsibility on the basis of the Commission's record, this will threaten our freedom. Therefore, it is extremely relevant as to what has been done to the CBC by this Government. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will give me the three minutes I lost because I would like to establish that it is an extremely relevant relationship that I have been trying to develop. Let the Minister of Communications understand that the CRTC cuts are not simply efficiencies to a bloated bureaucracy, as he seems to believe. I was pointing out that these cuts affect our native people. I stated that Our Native Land will not be returning as a program. I was saying that we should let the Minister of Communications tell our native people that this will not affect programming. The respected children's show, The Friendly Giant, will not be continued. Let the Minister of Communications tell Canadian children that CBC cuts will not affect programming.
The cuts have meant that the CBC cannot increase its participation in the Telefilm Fund. The Tories say: "Well, so what?". I will tell you what, Mr. Speaker, The CBC is the broadcast organization which has provided over 80 per cent of Telefilm projects with Canadian independent producers. If the CBC can no longer afford to co-fund with Telefilm, where will the independent sector find air time and dollars? Let the Government tell the Canadian independent film industry that the cuts will not affect programming.
There has been a major reversal of the traditional arm's length relationship between the Government and the CBC. It is no longer 1984, but it appears as if Big Brother is alive, well and living in Ottawa. The appointment of a troika of so-called consultants from outside to oversee the CBC and its cuts amounts to a major reversal of the traditional arm's length relationship between Parliament and cultural agencies such as the CBC. I am using the CBC as an illustration.
The Government cannot and should not tell newspapers what to print, nor should it tell the CBC what to do through the instrument of the CRTC. If the Government can tell the
February 1, 1985

CBC which dollars ought to be spent where or how, the Hon. Minister of Communications could in theory control the CBC.
I suspect that few Canadians knew that the Conservative Government's communications policy was to undermine what has been one of the most respected information services in the world.
This Government maintains that the CBC is inefficient and over-funded. Yet the Minister is reported to have expressed surprise at the results of his budget slashing, which has been the loss of 1,200 jobs. It appears as if the Minister and his appointed overseers had not foreseen this disastrous effect on the CBC.
What objective proof did the Minister have to justify the cuts to the CBC? A major study of the CBC by the McKinsey Management Consultants concluded that, compared to any other broadcaster in the world including the BBC and Australian and American broadcasters, the CBC is substantially more productive. They found that the CBC produces twice as much programming per employee while the cost is much lower. What is more, the CBC does the costly programming that the private network in the country will not do because it is not profitable to do so. That is why the CBC does the only drama, religious and science programming in Canadian television. The private industry will not undertake to provide Canadian information.
One must ask oneself if the Canadian television industry must face this cut of $85 million and possibly more. Why are the Tories doing this? Is there a sinister purpose? Certainly given the Government's activities in the last few months, there is a growing mistrust of a government policy which has apparently been shaped behind closed doors. Many of our talented young people are gathering around the country to ask what this policy will do in terms of their futures and in terms of the future of the arts and the sciences. What about their roles as young people?
I suggest that we are facing a very critical time. I wish to say on behalf of our arts and communications industries that there are people in Toronto, for example, who are seeing the loss of jobs of those who are paid by the CBC as well as those in allied industries and realizing that the whole cultural framework that is centered in that metropolis is being gravely threatened. I am told by my colleagues, not only on this side of the House but also on the other side, that in Montreal there is a large community that is extremely anxious, suffering and very concerned about its future as well.
I would like to conclude by saying that I would feel much more comfortable if in fact the Tories had not put forth these other policies during the past six months. This Bill would have made sense in the context of an arm's length relationship. I feel I must express my reservations and I feel that, under these circumstances, I cannot give my support to this Bill when I know that the Government is not able at the present time to give us a policy for an attitude and relationship with the arts community that would ensure that it would stay at arm's length, allow the Canadian identity to be protected, and not allow a collapse of our entire identity as Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I will keep my remarks brief and hope that one more speaker from the Liberal Opposition and perhaps my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) will be permitted a few moments to make the points they have in mind.
This Bill is intended to change the regulations of TV and radio broadcasting. It is intended to give the Minister power to regulate the content of what is broadcast by any "undertaking", as it is called, and also to define the "undertaking" so as to include most of those which are not now clearly enough licensed. It also undertakes to give authority to the CRTC to regulate the content with regard to any attacks upon the equality and dignity of any group, and that specifically includes any attacks related to sex. It also undertakes to regulate only the larger outlets and not the very small ones, although those are not defined clearly.
I believe my constituents, from what I have been told, would agree with the main thrust of this Bill. The people of Spadina are patriotic people whether they were born here or came here from other countries. They want to see news of Canada. They want to see a variety of Canada represented on TV and on radio by the CBC and by other stations. They do not want to be fed exclusively with what comes from across the border or from overseas. They recognize, therefore, the need to have the Canadian state regulate what is otherwise capable of being monopolized by one private point of view. In that respect, they appreciate the state enterprise created by the Tories half a century ago. Some of my constituents recognize that as a very positive forerunner of socialism.
There are some defects in this program, however. This Bill does little to deal with the question of violence on TV. It gets closer to it but does not get very far. It also leaves the way open for total deregulation, which we know is in the philosophy
February 1, 1985

of Reaganomics, which philosophy is espoused by the Government at the present time. That is a worrisome matter and leaves undefined the question of services to small communities, although perhaps there is a task force report which will deal with that subject.
As has been pointed out, this Bill does nothing to offset the danger to Canadian content, the danger of losing the presentation of Canadian news, lifestyle, drama and music. There is the danger of destroying that opportunity through the budget cuts which have previously been referred to and which, as you have said, Mr. Speaker, have in fact become part of this debate. I agree with your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that they do belong to this debate, certainly from the point of view of the people in the constituency of Spadina.
There are many people in Spadina who earn their living, albeit a very small one, by producing programs not only for the CBC but for the private producers on radio and on TV. No amount of careful regulation under this new Bill will ensure that they can make their contribution as Chinese, Portuguese, British, Irish or native people, whoever they may be. No amount of regulation will make sure that they can make their contribution if the whole of the funding for the work they do is destroyed by the budget cuts of this Government. We will be hearing more from them in the next few weeks, Mr. Speaker, because they are organizing with others in this country to present their views publicly. I will therefore not take any more time to present their view today, but I will be back.

Mr. Speaker, I have some concern about the Bill before us and I have discussed one or two of them with the Parliamentary Secretary, who was very forthcoming regarding the intent of this legislation. The amendments to the CRTC Act will give the Governor in Council the power to direct the Commission on policy matters. My concern lies with the procedural safeguards.
For those regarding the tabling of documentation, referral to committee and the time period, I commend the Government. I think it is important that Members of Parliament, regardless of political faith or ideology, have an opportunity to discuss in great detail the changes the Government might wish to bring forward. There is no better avenue than the floor of the House of Commons or the committee rooms.
Concerning the amendments to the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act, I am happy to see that the CRTC will have a clear mandate for dealing with all types of abusive programming. I hope that, notwithstanding the statements regarding sexually abusive programming, this will cover violence as well. Notwithstanding the desire of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to make Canada the fifty-first state, we are quite different from the U.S. I think a lot of that has to do with our programming. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in the U.S. there is a very great and sophisticated lobby to maintain the public broadcasting system. I hope that in Canada we will
CRTC Act
continue with an enriched CBC in the future and with its quality programs. In this respect, I hope the Government will very clearly spell out to the CRTC its policy direction on abusive programming. Other Members have alluded to the violence we see on television, particularly in rock videos. A number of programs and videos are quite damaging. However, I am optimistic that the necessary and all-encompassing policy direction will be forthcoming.
The other amendments to the Broadcasting Act are designed to reduce the burden of broadcasting regulation on the private sector. I applaud that intention, but one thing did concern me and I raised it with the Parliamentary Secretary. CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House the government should amend the Constitution Act 1982, to include property rights and, that the Governor General issue a Proclamation under the Great Seal of Canada to amend section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights so that it reads as follows:
"7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice." and this House urges that the Legislative Assemblies of all provinces and the Senate pass similar resolutions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if the good people in Ottawa would drink more of that Similkameen wine they would soon be able to identify the region and associate the quality of debate that comes from this desk with the quality of that wine.
I wish to acknowledge the cogency of what the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) has said about the entrenchment of the right of enjoyment of property in previous remarks in the House. I have the greatest respect for him and I know that we share the concern for the protection of property rights. It is a concern that farmers in all of our constituencies have expressed to us in earnest terms. This has not only been expressed by farmers but, since I am a farmer, I refer to those good citizens of Canada.
Private Members' Hour provides an opportunity to discuss, in a general way, some of the issues arising out of the idea of entrenching property rights in the Constitution. However, I do not believe that Private Members' Hour is suitable for resolving a matter of such significance. This is so, even though it is my wish that the property rights should be entrenched in the Constitution. It must be recognized that there are many individuals and groups, as well as provinces, who have expressed reservations about the entrenchment of property rights. In that context, it does not seem to me that it is appropriate to make decisions about this matter during Private Members' Hour.
I emphasize my support and the support of my Party for the entrenchment of property rights. It bears repeating that it was the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, the late former Prime Minister and Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, who introduced the Canadian Bill of Rights in 1960. As a result, the right of enjoyment of property is protected at the federal level in Canada.
Since that time, the Progressive Conservative Party has supported the entrenchment of property rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As a matter of fact, we lobbied to have property rights included in the Charter when it was first established. We have continued to advocate its inclusion.
We in the Progressive Conservative Party believe that property and the right to enjoy it are essential features of our democratic society. These features, among others, distinguish our society from totalitarian countries. The well-being of our country is not dependent solely on government. In Canada,

February 1, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
government, business, individuals and others are economic partners. We want to retain that system.
At the basis of our ability as individuals to participate in this partnership and contribute to the well-being of our country, is the right to own and enjoy property and the right to employ our property in our business enterprises. Our business enterprises, whether large or small, are the backbone of our economy and they are owned by individual Canadians.
These individuals provide the resources and the capital upon which these enterprises depend. In this context, the comments of Professor Jack Knetsch of Simon Fraser University are particularly apt. I quote the following from page one of his book Property Rights and Compensation:
In most societies a system of entitlements has evolved which, among other effects, largely assures that the rewards to productive effort are returned to those making the effort and are not gratuitously appropriated by others. This "sowing and reaping" rationale remains, in most communities, a major protection for investment and an important incentive for the efficient use of resources. Entitlements that encourage individuals to husband property, and individuals' efforts to obtain further advantage, provide gains for the community.
I suggest that it is appropriate to note that the socialist philosophy of state ownership which is espoused by the NDP provides the exact opposite, a disincentive to progress and economic development.
The right to own and enjoy property allows us to enjoy the fruits of our endeavours whether we are self-employed or wage earners. It enables us to own automobiles, homes and farms and to have the sort of things we need to carry on the good life that we enjoy in Canada. Our right to own and enjoy property gives us a stake in our country. It is important then that property rights should receive adequate protection, and that means entrenching them in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Entrenching property rights would mean that they would not be dependent on the good-will of the government of the day. The Charter is now the supreme law of the land. The tradition of the supremacy of Parliament has been altered. The actions of government are now subject to the scrutiny of the courts which are charged with interpreting and enforcing the Charter. It is, however, precisely for this reason that the entrenchment of property rights requires careful consideration. The consequences of entrenching property rights are potentially far-reaching.
Many individuals and groups as well as provinces have expressed sincere concerns about the possible consequences of entrenching property rights. This concern must be recognized and dealt with. In this connection I would note that the federal Government cannot by itself entrench property rights in the Constitution. Amending the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to entrench property rights would require resolutions of the legislative assemblies of at least seven provinces with at least 50 per cent of the population. To date, however, only two provinces, British Columbia and New Brunswick, have passed resolutions supporting the entrenchment of property rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Other
provinces have expressed some reluctance to support the entrenchment of property rights. That is why we say that perhaps a Private Members Motion is not the best way to ensure that full consideration and negotiation is established before this is entered into.
The provinces are concerned that by entrenching property rights we will enable the courts to interfere with laws which protect important societal interests. As examples of this the provinces cite land use planning and municipal laws, environmental laws, resource laws, real and personal property laws, building and health and safety laws, and other types of laws. They ask, for instance, whether an entrenched right to the enjoyment of property might affect their ability to control the use of privately-owned land in order to protect the environment or to protect communities. Their concerns are sincere and deserve consideration.
I believe that the provinces are open-minded on this matter. Because their support is necessary if we are to entrench property rights, we should be working together with them to see if we can resolve their concerns in a way that is acceptable to all interested parties. We should be attempting to build a consensus on this matter, adopting the co-operative and conciliatory approach to federalism which is the hallmark of the new Government of Canada.
There is another reason for taking this sort of approach. Subsection 38(2) of the new Constitution, that is, the Constitution Act, 1982, allows a province to opt out of a constitutional amendment which "derogates from the legislative powers, the proprietary rights or any other rights or privileges of the legislature or government of a province". It would appear that a property rights amendment would undoubtedly come within Subsection 38(2). It is possible then that acting in an untimely fashion might prompt a disaffected province to opt out of a property rights amendment, which would be its right. It is surely our responsibility to avoid the resulting inconsistent application of property rights protections across the country. Doing so requires us to endeavour to reach a consensus on this matter.
Not only the provinces are concerned about the effects of entrenching property rights. Women's groups are apprehensive that the entrenchment of property rights may jeopardize the interests of women as they have emerged in recent family law reform. These reforms were intended to recognize as equal the contributions of homemakers and breadwinners to the family. They do so by providing for a presumptive equal division of assets when a marriage breaks down. The courts may award assets to one spouse even where the other spouse has the apparent legal title. Women's groups are afraid that constitutional property rights guarantees might prevent a court from doing this, with a resulting adverse impact on women. Even if the courts were ultimately to uphold these matrimonial property laws, women's groups are concerned that women will have to bear the cost and hardship of fighting the cases which will inevitably arise under a constitutional property rights guarantee. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women
February 1, 1985

dealt with the matter of the entrenchment of property rights in a resolution dated September 27, 1983. It reads in part:
Whereas on March 29, 1983, an amendment to Article 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, concerning property rights, was introduced in the House of Commons and was defeated;
Whereas a second similar amendment may be introduced;
Whereas the aim of the amendment of March 29, 1983, was to protect property rights in the traditional sense of the word, meaning primarily real property;
Whereas Canadian women in general, are not owners of real property and, furthermore, own relatively little property of any kind;
Whereas the probable consequences of such an amendment have not been sufficiently studied and discussed;
Whereas such an amendment could have grave consequences on the rights which women have already obtained, such as the right to division of the matrimonial home;
Whereas any increased protection of property in the Canadian Constitution must also protect new types of property, which are often social rights and benefits such as rent control, pensions and labour standards;
The CACSW recommends to the federal government that no new amendment be introduced in the House of Commons before an in-depth study can be made to establish the consequences of such a measure on the lives of Canadian women. We also ask that any such measure be submitted to the general public so that Canadian women be given the chance to voice their opinion on the matter.
It seems to me that these are sincere concerns that have to be considered. Women's groups appear to be open-minded on these issues. We should make an effort to resolve their concerns. The opportunity to do so should not be forgone.
Even assuming that we can reach a consensus on the entrenchment of property rights, it remains for us to settle the form of the protection. Even the two provinces which have passed resolutions to entrench property rights have not agreed upon the form that such a constitutional amendment should take. We have more than just the ancient and historic reasons for entrenching property rights. This nation, Canada, is a signatory to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. We as a nation are a signatory. Therefore, I believe none of us can stand in the House and oppose that. What does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights state? Article 17 reads:
(1)	Everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others.

We often see members of the New Democratic Party standing and quoting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. I often wonder why they selectively skip over Article 17. It is because fundamentally they do not believe in property rights. We cannot have security of the person, liberty and freedom without property rights. When people have property rights, the chance to work and create, they create their own pension plans. They can then turn up their noses at power, bureaucrats and Governments because they can look after themselves. This is why it is critical. That is the difference between western and eastern democracies.
Another step in that ancient trail was the Canadian Bill of Rights. Everyone should read Article (l)(a). Several provinces have statutory Bills of Rights which talk about the right to property, but there is a major difference. A statute is a statute. It can be changed overnight. Once it is entrenched and becomes part of the fundamental law, it cannot then be arbitrarily taken away by Governments that might be responding to the immediate heat of the day rather than to the long-term good of the people. Therefore, having decided as a nation to go into an entrenched Charter with all it means in terms of the transfer of power to the courts, I say that we should have all of it.
Why was it not in the Constitution Act, 1982? It is a sad story, because for a few hours it was there. Coming from a riding where there are many native groups, I find they are also worried about how property rights can affect their land claims and land entitlement. Those groups add their concern to the voice of women. Labour groups have expressed concerns about how the rights of workers will be affected versus those who own property.
When I spoke of this type of proposal on the previous occasion, I read from an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of July 1983. A representative of mortgage holders explained why he wanted property rights in the Constitution. He stated that because a mortgage is considered property, he would have more rights than a worker or others who may make claims on the assets of a company which had gone bankrupt. That is a legitimate concern. He was speaking for his industry and his special interest group. He said that, as a mortgage holder, someone who had lent money to a company, he had more
Constitution Act, 1982
rights than did the workers who had given their labour. There is somebody from the other side explaining why they want property rights in the Constitution.
Environmental groups have spoken about their concerns and what kinds of laws can be passed in this land if property rights are in the Constitution. More important, Conservative provincial Governments right across this nation have said that they do not want property rights in the Constitution. It is not 30 New Democrats in the House of Commons who are preventing or have prevented in the past property rights from being in the Constitution. It is the Premier of Alberta and the Premiers of other Conservative Governments across this land.
Members do not have to take my word. They can check the word of various Conservative provincial spokesmen. As the mover of the motion is from Alberta, I will use the example of his own provincial Government. Mr. Horseman, the Minister of Inter-Governmental Affairs of that Province, said:
It is made clear that the Government of Alberta's position is that the Constitutional responsibility for property and civil rights is that of the provinces. It should properly remain there and not be entrenched in the Charter of Rights and thus become subject to any control by the federal Government.
I do not know Mr. Horseman personally. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) does. I presume they are friends and colleagues. I presume the Hon. Member was not calling his provincial colleague a socialist. I further presume it was that man's responsibility to speak for the Government of Alberta. The official position of that provincial Conservative Government is that it does not want it in the Constitution. Don't blame us, blame your colleagues. The Government of Alberta is not alone. I further quote Mr. Horseman:
After a brief survey of other provinces by the Province of Alberta, it was clear that there was very little support given by other provinces for inclusion of the subject of property rights in the Charter.
The time period in which they spoke was very similar to the present time period. Almost every one of those provincial Governments is led by a Conservative administration. Let us not play politics. Let us be honest with each other. Let us tell the truth about who is really opposing property rights as an entrenched part of our Constitution. If we could resolve the other concerns which I expressed, the concerns about the environment, the concerns about the provinces' ability to regulate the use of land within their jurisdictions; if we could make sure that we could protect the ability of provincial Governments to make sure that farm land is owned by residents of the provinces, by people who are actually working the farms; if we could protect the rights of women, and if we could prove that the right to property is not a right that is more equal than the rights of the workers, then there is nothing wrong with property rights being entrenched in the Constitution. However, if property rights will be put in the Constitution as rights which would make one group of Canadians more powerful and will give one group of Canadians more rights and more privileges than others, then it is a problem.
